title: TF upgrade edge-case & runtime smoke notes
content:
Context / intent:
This is a working note for oddball failures we've seen during Private deployments upgrades (TF module, runtime image, kernel/NVIDIA driver changes). The goal is: 1) capture reproducible signals and heuristics, 2) provide a compact smoke checklist to run post-upgrade, and 3) record quick rollback/mitigation steps so on-call can triage faster.

Status: draft - leaning towards operational checklist + short tech notes. Not exhaustive. Use this during the next staging -> customer upgrade window; we'll iterate.

Quick summary of common failure classes we've hit (edge cases):
- Node fails to join cluster after TF apply: usually caused by subnet/route table mismatch, MTU misconfig, or cloud-init timingouts.
- Pods repeatedly CrashLoopBackOff: caused by cgroup v2 host/container mismatch, container runtime upgrades (containerd vs docker shim), or missing kernel features required by our runtime (e.g., memfd_create flags).
- Runtime cannot allocate GPU/KV cache: driver/user-space mismatch (nvidia-driver vs cuda libs vs rpms) or device plugin failing to register.
- High inference latency / long tail after upgrade: new kernel or scheduling changes (IRQ affinity, cpufreq governors), or automated batching misconfiguration from new config.
- DNS failures inside pods / control plane: iptables vs nftables differences after OS upgrades, or VPC's DNS resolver policies changed by cloud provider.

Pre-upgrade notes (Terraform + infra):
- Pin provider versions in modules: e.g. terraform { required_providers { aws = ">= 4.0, < 5.0" } } - avoid sudden provider API/behaviour changes.
- Lock module versions in private registry or use git tags for modules.
- Always run terraform plan -out=plan.tfplan and keep plan artifact attached to run for audit.
- Validate state lock: ensure remote state lock is functioning (S3+Dynamo or GCS with lock).
- Snapshot critical VMs or take AMI images (or equivalent) before OS/kernel changes.
- If changing MTU or VPC CIDR: plan a small rolling test cluster first; these network changes are high-risk.
- Document provider feature flags that might change (e.g., AWS VPC DNS settings) in upgrade playbook.

Preflight quick commands (run on a representative node and control plane):
- uname -a
- cat /etc/os-release
- lsmod | grep nvidia || true
- nvidia-smi --query-gpu=driver_version,name --format=csv,noheader || true
- systemctl status redwood-runtime.service || journalctl -u redwood-runtime.service -n 200 --no-pager
- docker info || containerd --version || crictl --version
- ip link show | grep mtu
- dig @127.0.0.1 my-service.svc.cluster.local +short || nslookup my-service.default.svc.cluster.local 127.0.0.53
- cat /proc/cgroups || stat -fc %T /sys/fs/cgroup
- sudo dmesg | tail -n 200 | egrep -i "oom|nvidia|gpu|nvlink|IOMMU|kernel panic"

Smoke-test checklist (run after TF apply and runtime deploy):
1) Node health & join checks (10m)
   - kubectl get nodes --no-headers -o wide: ensure new nodes Ready within 3 minutes.
   - If NotReady > 5m: check kubelet logs (journalctl -u kubelet) and /var/log/cloud-init-output.log for provisioning errors.
2) Basic runtime health (5m)
   - curl -sS http://localhost:4317/health or runtime health endpoint: expect 200 and small JSON {"status":"ok"}.
   - systemctl status redwood-runtime.service -> active (running) within 1m of service start.
3) Inference sanity (5m)
   - Run single-token prompt: run local smoke script that hits runtime with a 16-token prompt; check response shape and latency < 200ms median.
   - Run embedding request: 3 requests -> consistent dims and no errors.
4) GPU allocation (5m)
   - nvidia-smi shows processes from container runtime.
   - Check device plugin logs (kube-system): kubectl -n kube-system logs ds/nvidia-device-plugin - tail 100.
5) KV cache + cold start caching (10m)
   - Send identical prompt twice; second call should be faster and not recompile model or warm weights (confirm via runtime logs: "cache hit" lines).
6) Load-light tail tests (15m)
   - Fire a small burst (50 concurrent lightweight completions) using the test harness. Monitor 95th/99th latency; if 95p > 2x baseline or 99p spikes, open incident.
7) Network/DNS verification (5m)
   - From a pod: curl http://169.254.169.254/ to verify metadata access if required.
   - Ensure cluster DNS resolves backend services consistently across AZs.

Common troubleshooting flows and signals (rapid heuristics):
- Node NotReady + kubelet crashloop: check /var/lib/kubelet/ directory full, or wrong kubelet config after TF changed kubelet flags. Check cgroup driver mismatch: container runtime uses cgroup v1 but kubelet expects cgroup v2.
- Pods OOMKilled after upgrade: new kernel changed overcommit settings or sysctl; check /proc/sys/vm/overcommit_memory and runtime limits (cgroups). Look for hugepages changes.
- GPU visible to OS but not to pods: device plugin failing; examine nvidia-container-runtime and runtime.json that maps runc config. Check LD_LIBRARY_PATH in runtime container image - mismatched libc/cuda lib versions common after distro upgrades.
- Persistent DNS timeouts post-upgrade: inspect iptables vs nftables rules; running new systemd-resolved versions can change resolver socket (127.0.0.53) semantics. Fall back test: run dig +trace from node to cluster DNS.

Terraform/Module-specific gotchas and notes:
- Terraform resource replacement semantics: if you rename a resource or change immutable field, module may recreate subnets which briefly detach route tables -> ephemeral control-plane disconnections. Use lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true } for critical resources where appropriate, or schedule maintenance window.
- Module inputs that silently change instance types: double-check defaults for the next version of the module. We had a case where instance_profile default changed producing T3 -> C6g.
- Provider version skew between root module and child modules can cause plan/apply mismatches. Enforce workspace-level required_providers and run tflint/terraform validate in CI.
- Terraform apply can reorder provider operations in edge cases. Keep plan artifacts and use apply -parallelism=1 for risky infra (network or route changes) during upgrades.

Rollback triggers (immediate) - if any of these observed within smoke window:
- New nodes failing to join cluster and >30% of cluster NotReady -> rollback TF and stop rollout.
- >25% increase in 95p latency or any regression in 99p for inference -> rollback runtime image.
- Repeated CrashLoopBackOff of runtime pods with same stack trace -> rollback runtime image or restore prior config.
- Missing GPU allocations across >1 node -> rollback driver/runtime change.

Quick rollback playbook (manual):
1) Pause automation/orchestration: stop any automated canary promotion.
2) Revert TF plan: terraform apply previous_plan.tfplan OR revert git commit for modules and run plan+apply. If plan artifact available prefer it.
3) Re-deploy prior runtime image tag: update deployment to previous image and watch pods restart.
4) If networking changed (MTU/CIDR) and cannot revert: spin up a rollback cluster from snapshot and migrate traffic.
5) Notify on-call and customers with short summary + ETA.

Log pointers and what to capture for post-mortem:
- journalctl -u redwood-runtime.service -n 500 > runtime-journal.log
- kubectl get events --all-namespaces --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp > events-after-upgrade.txt
- docker/containerd runtime logs from node: /var/log/docker.log or /var/log/containers/*runtime*.log
- dmesg to capture kernel OOPS or GPU driver errors
- /var/log/cloud-init-output.log and cloud provider instance event logs
- tfstate snapshot and the plan artifact used in apply

Hypothesis checklist (for investigation):
- If symptoms mention "device not found" and dmesg shows nvlink errors -> suspect physical GPU health or driver upgrade mismatch. Reboot one node and revalidate.
- If symptoms are "DNS lookup slow/timeout" after OS kernel update -> suspect nftables/iptables translation; check kernel conntrack table sizes and systemd-resolved version change.
- If pods never reach Running with image pull errors -> registry permissions or new image signed with different keys (image trust).

Notes to future self / TODOs:
- Create automated smoke job in CI to run the checklist automatically and create a pass/fail attestation after each TF apply in staging.
- Add explicit provider and module pins to the private-registry README.
- Build small helper script that collects the preflight commands above and uploads to an S3 run artifact – saves time during incidents.
- Add a short KB entry for Nvidia-driver + CUDA compatibility matrix we prefer for on-prem images.

Appendix: quick commands to run during triage (copy-paste)
- kubectl get nodes -o wide
- journalctl -u kubelet -n 200 --no-pager
- journalctl -u redwood-runtime -n 200 --no-pager
- sudo systemctl restart redwood-runtime && sleep 10 && systemctl status redwood-runtime
- sudo nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,name,utilization.gpu,driver_version --format=csv,noheader
- sudo cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward; ip link show | egrep -i "mtu|state"
- terraform init -upgrade=false; terraform plan -out=plan.tfplan

End of doc - iterate after using in next upgrade window.
